title: Microenterprise credit can create customer surplus beyond the borrowing firm
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35729 randomized evaluation of large loans to microenterprises in Chile, with treated firms, customer surveys, and a market comparison of more than 125,000 non-treated firms
geography: Chile; comparative international evidence used to test a firm-credit-to-consumer-welfare mechanism, not a U.S. estimate

observations.period: Working paper issued September 2026; randomized loan expansion and customer outcomes in Chile

denominator.unit: more than 125,000 non-treated firms operating in the same markets; exact count not stated in abstract

treated_firm_profit.unit: USD per month increase in treated-firm profits

customer_surplus.unit: USD per month gain in customer consumer surplus

business_stealing.value: little evidence of business stealing among non-treated firms in the same markets

observations.method: Randomized controlled trial of large loans to microenterprises, paired with customer survey data and a comparison of more than 125,000 non-treated firms in the same markets.
observations.uncertainty: The source is a working paper and the abstract does not disclose the customer-survey denominator, loan terms, exact randomization unit, confidence intervals, or all mechanisms producing consumer surplus. Chilean market and firm conditions may not generalize to U.S. consumers or lenders.
observations.subgroup: Treated microenterprises, their customers, and non-treated firms operating in the same Chilean markets; customer-level heterogeneity is not available in the abstract.
observations.counterinterpretation: Customer surplus may reflect improved variety, quality, availability, prices, convenience, or relationships rather than a uniform gain for all customers. Limited business stealing does not establish equal access, durable firm survival, worker gains, or long-run market competition.

boundary: This comparative record adds a credit-to-firm-to-customer-welfare pathway. It does not establish a U.S. consumer effect, a universal microenterprise-credit result, worker benefit, durable firm survival, or long-run inequality change.
